narrative: The model estimated a 72.5% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—roughly a three-in-four risk—so your application was denied on the basis of that high predicted risk. The strongest factor was your third-year class standing: at 1.00, it was far from the accepted-student average of about 5.79, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class standing, also 1.00 versus an accepted average near 6.00, was the second most influential factor and likewise increased the failure estimate. Your undergraduate GPA, 3.20 compared with the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor, but it slightly pushed toward passing; it was not enough to offset the two class-standing signals. Gender and race were not used in the prediction. Next, contact admissions to ask whether feedback or reconsideration is available and whether you can submit additional evidence. Meet a pre-law advisor to address the academic pattern behind the class standings, consider whether retaking the LSAT or additional coursework would strengthen your record, and apply to programs that review applicants holistically and offer bar-preparation support.
